question.text: Does evidence-based practice improve patient outcomes?
question.context: Evidence-based practice (EBP) is widely promoted, but does EBP produce better patient outcomes? We report a natural experiment when part of the internal medicine service in a hospital was reorganized in 2003 to form an EBP unit, the rest of the service remaining unchanged. The units attended similar patients until 2012 permitting comparisons of outcomes and activity. We used routinely collected statistics (2004-11) to compare the two different methods of practice and test whether patients being seen by the EBP unit differed from standard practice (SP) patients. Data were available by doctor and year. To check for differences between the EBP and SP doctors prior to reorganization, we used statistics from 2000 to 2003. We looked for changes in patient outcomes or activity following reorganization and whether the EBP unit was achieving significantly different results from SP. Data across the periods were combined and tested using Mann-Whitney test. No statistically significant differences in outcomes were detected between the EBP and the SP doctors prior to reorganization. Following the unit's establishment, the mortality of patients being treated by EBP doctors compared with their previous performance dropped from 7.4% to 6.3% (P < 0.02) and length of stay from 9.15 to 6.01 days (P = 0.002). No statistically significant improvements were seen in SP physicians' performance. No differences in the proportion of patients admitted or their complexity between the services were detected. Despite this, EBP patients had a clinically significantly lower risk of death 6.27% versus 7.75% (P < 0.001) and a shorter length of stay 6.01 versus 8.46 days (P < 0.001) than SP patients. Readmission rates were similar: 14.4% (EBP); 14.5% (SP). EBP doctors attended twice as many patients/doctor as SP doctors.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates a statistically significant improvement in patient outcomes (mortality and length of stay) for patients treated by the EBP unit compared to standard practice. The improvements were clinically significant and not observed in the standard practice group. This suggests that EBP does improve patient outcomes.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: EBP patients had a clinically significantly lower risk of death 6.27% versus 7.75% (P < 0.001) and a shorter length of stay 6.01 versus 8.46 days (P < 0.001) than SP patients.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the EBP unit saw twice as many patients per doctor, the improved outcomes suggest that the increased volume did not negate the benefits of EBP. The lack of difference in admission rates or complexity between the two groups further supports the conclusion that EBP is effective.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The data shows statistically significant improvements in mortality (7.4% to 6.3%, P<0.02) and length of stay (9.15 to 6.01 days, P=0.002) for EBP patients compared to SP patients. These results demonstrate that evidence-based practice is associated with better clinical outcomes.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The 6.27% mortality rate and 6.01-day length of stay for EBP patients versus 7.75% mortality and 8.46-day length of stay for SP patients (both P<0.001) provide strong evidence of improved outcomes with EBP.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates statistically and clinically significant improvements in mortality and length of stay for patients treated by the EBP unit compared to standard practice, despite no pre-reorganization differences. The improvements were sustained and not seen in the control group, indicating EBP positively impacts outcomes.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: EBP patients had a clinically significantly lower risk of death (6.27% vs 7.75%, P<0.001) and shorter length of stay (6.01 vs 8.46 days, P<0.001) than SP patients.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered 'maybe' due to lack of statistical significance in some metrics, but ruled out as the clinically significant improvements in mortality and LOS outweighed this, and no confounding factors (e.g., patient complexity) were detected.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Possible confounders such as differences in patient populations or comorbidities were not found, but the key improvement in outcomes by the EBP group post-reorganization strongly supports the effectiveness of EBP in this context.
